skillSays: Import from three/webgpu and three/tsl, and await renderer.init() before touching the renderer.
Write shaders as TSL node graphs in JavaScript (Fn, uniform, method chaining) on the NodeMaterial slots: colorNode, positionNode, emissiveNode, opacityNode.
GPU particles use storage buffers plus Fn(...)().compute(count), run with renderer.compute().
Inside TSL, plain JS reassignment is invisible to the graph: use .assign(), .toVar() or select().
Handle device loss, and remember WebGPURenderer can fall back to a WebGL 2 backend.
Prefer built-in post-processing and node materials over hand-written WGSL unless needed.

changes: The orb's wobble, fresnel rim and colors are TSL nodes (mx_noise_float into positionNode, a view-angle fresnel into colorNode and emissiveNode); the slot ring is one InstancedMesh animated per instance on the GPU with instanceIndex and time, no JS per frame
The renderer is created with await init() and a try order of WebGPU then forced WebGL 2; the same TSL material graph rendered on both (checked with ?renderer=webgl)
A device.lost handler reloads once instead of leaving a dead canvas
On real WebGPU a compute shader integrates each particle (spring toward its slot, noise drift while unsettled) in storage buffers; sprites read positions straight from the buffer

WebGPU was available in this headless Chrome. When the backend is WebGL 2 the page switches to a fallback path that computes the same scatter-to-grid motion in the vertex stage from instanced attributes, so it still renders (checked with ?renderer=webgl)
The TSL gotcha is respected: buffer elements use addAssign / mulAssign, no JS variable reassignment inside the shader

notes: Pinned to three@0.170.0 per the brief. That release has no instancedArray helper or three.tsl.js (TSL is exported from three.webgpu.js), so storage(new StorageInstancedBufferAttribute(...)) is used, which is the same idea. WebGL 2 fallback is a vertex-stage path, not compute.
